title: Passover: your own question
hookLine: many families add their own readings and questions
tomorrow: why is the same flat bread called sad and free?

lines: A NEW VERSE IN AN OLD SONG.
cards: A singer covers an old song and slips in a new verse. Half the comments love it. The other half want the original, untouched, the way their parents played it.
Families have the same argument over the seder. Can you add your own question to a script that old? Inside the tradition there are two real answers, and both come from people who love the Haggadah.

teach.b: Both start from one line in the Haggadah: whoever tells more of the going out from Egypt is praiseworthy.
And from the Mishnah's frame for the night: begin with the shame and end with the praise, and teach each child by their understanding. The first view says: keep the words.
The fixed text is what links this table to tables long ago and far away; a guest from anywhere can find the page.

teach.h: KEEP THE WORDS; TALK AROUND THEM.
teach.b: Telling more happens in the talk around the words, in questions, arguments, stories from your own family. The book stays the book.

teach.h: WRITE IT IN; BRING THIS YEAR.
teach.b: The second view says: write it in.
Some families add their own readings, a cup for Miriam, a poem, a question about who isn't free yet today.

The Mishnah already bends the telling to the people at the table, they say, by teaching each child by their understanding. A new reading is how this year's table gets into the story. Notice what the two views share.
Neither wants a quiet seder. Neither thinks the questions are only for kids.
The disagreement is about where your question lives: spoken around the old words, or printed on the page. Either way, the night is built for one more question.

how: Some Jewish families keep the traditional Haggadah text and add only through discussion; others add readings, poems or new symbols such as a cup for Miriam. Both keep the seder's frame and its questions.

s: adding a new reading to the seder is forbidden
some families add readings; others keep the words fixed and add in the talk. both views live inside the tradition.
the Haggadah praises whoever tells more of the exodus story
both sides of the debate start from that line.
families who keep the fixed text don't ask new questions
they ask them in the talk around the words; the book stays the book.

games.q: your aunt wants to read a new poem at the seder. Saba says keep the Haggadah's words. give Saba's side its best case.
o: the old words link this table to every table before it; new ideas can live in the talk.
new readings break the rules of the seder, so they can't be allowed.
a poem is fine, as long as it's read in Hebrew and not in English.
games.why: both sides want questions at the table. Saba's view keeps the page fixed so anyone, anywhere, can find it, and lets the talk carry what's new.

practice: Write one question you'd ask at a seder this year, by hand, on a card or the back of an envelope. Make it a real one, something you actually wonder about freedom, or leaving, or your own family.
Read it to yourself once, then fold the card in half; it's ready for the table.

wordCard.voice: Passover: the festival of the exodus, where the telling has a fixed frame and room for one more question.

orig.note: Hebrew: what is different? the opening words of the seder's questions.

carryVoice: Something to keep: add your question, in the talk around the page or on the page itself. Until tomorrow.
